lead.topic: Chromosome and centromere evolution in pig pan-genomes
lead.headline: Pig Y chromosomes reveal moving centromeres
lead.deck: Complete pig genomes reveal that even the chromosome's cell-division attachment site can shift across lineages.
lead.authors: Feng Y, Du H, Zhang J, Ma Y, Lu S, et al., Liu J
paragraphs: A centromere is the chromosome region where the machinery of cell division attaches. Its DNA is often so repetitive that genome assemblies leave it unfinished. Yu Feng and colleagues assembled three pig genomes from telomere to telomere, meaning from one chromosome end to the other, and another 16 high-quality genomes. With 12 Y-chromosome assemblies and maps of centromere-binding proteins, they could compare these difficult regions across breeds rather than rely on a single reference animal. They found that the position of the Y centromere varies among lineages, alongside changes in nearby repeated DNA.

The team also detected changing centromere positions on chromosome 1. A highly expressed gene, eEF1A1, sits near these regions and near rearrangement breakpoints in several mammals, making it a candidate link between transcription and chromosome fragility, not proof of causation. Their wider pan-genome, which combines variants across individuals, improved estimates of inherited trait variation. Experiments on AKR1B1 offered a possible connection between a regulatory insertion and tolerance of low oxygen. The broad lesson extends beyond pigs: fully assembling repetitive chromosomes can reveal evolutionary variation concealed by conventional reference genomes, while the proposed causes of that variation still require tests.
lead.push: Sequence and map centromere-binding proteins in wild and domestic pigs sampled across the same geographic regions. Does Y-centromere position track shared ancestry, repeat-array length, or domestication after those factors are separated? Test whether changing eEF1A1 transcription alters chromosome breakage instead of assuming a nearby active gene caused the rearrangements.

people.name: Yu Feng
people.bio: Yu Feng is a genomics researcher and postdoctoral fellow at China Agricultural University in Beijing. His professional site lists a PhD in genomics from the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Institute of Zoology and earlier training in animal genetics. His research spans centromere evolution, comparative genomes and functional genomics.

people.name: Jianfeng Liu
people.bio: Jianfeng Liu is a professor of animal genetics and breeding at China Agricultural University. His laboratory studies quantitative genetics, bioinformatics, livestock genomics and complex traits. He earned his PhD at China Agricultural University and completed postdoctoral training at the University of Missouri–Kansas City School of Medicine, according to his institutional biography.

slot2.headline: Random chance joins natural selection
slot2.body: In 1931, Sewall Wright put mutation, natural selection, migration and genetic drift into a shared mathematical description of changing gene frequencies. Drift is random change caused by finite population size, not selection for a useful trait. Wright showed how population size and movement among groups can change evolutionary outcomes. He also imagined populations moving across an adaptive landscape of alternative genetic combinations. Later work, including Motoo Kimura's diffusion theory, built on Wright's mathematics. His proposed shifting-balance route to adaptation remains debated, but the paper still supplies much of the language and mathematical foundation of population genetics.

slot3.headline: Optics can steer information independently of light
slot3.cite: Weimar et al., Nature Materials (16 Nov 2026), Controlling the flow of information in optical metrology.
slot3.body: Light carries energy, but does it carry useful measurement information along the same routes? A study published in Nature Materials on November 16 uses mathematical analysis and numerical simulations to show why the answer can be no. Fisher information describes how precisely measurements can estimate an unknown property, such as a nanoparticle's position. The researchers model its flow around scattering objects and show resonance, interference, diffraction and even vortices, sometimes unlike the energy flow. This suggests new ways to design illumination, nearby structures and detectors for better precision. The paper demonstrates a theoretical framework and modeled examples, not a deployed instrument's performance gain.
